title: Jakob Fugger Buys an Election
text:
When Emperor Maximilian died in January 1519, seven German electors had to choose his successor as Holy Roman Emperor. The two main candidates were Maximilian's grandson Charles, already king of Spain, and Francis I of France. Both sides knew the vote would go to whoever paid the electors most, and the bribes had to be in cash or reliable credit.

Jakob Fugger of Augsburg, the richest banker of his age, had long financed the Habsburgs. He backed Charles and refused to provide money for the French. Fugger's house supplied the larger part of the roughly 850,000 florins Charles spent on the election, with other bankers providing the rest. In June 1519 the electors unanimously chose Charles, who became Emperor Charles V.

Charles was slow to repay. In 1523 Fugger wrote him a famous letter. He reminded the emperor that it was well known that without Fugger's help he could not have obtained the imperial crown, and that the electors' own letters proved it. He asked politely but firmly for his money with interest. Charles arranged repayment, partly by granting the Fuggers rights to income from Spanish mines and lands. The family's fortunes remained bound to the Habsburgs for decades.
lesson: Timing makes money powerful: support given when someone needs it most buys lasting leverage. Remember that the same dependence can tie the lender to the borrower.
people: Jakob Fugger, Charles V, Francis I
source: Jakob Fugger, letter to Charles V (April 1523); Greg Steinmetz, The Richest Man Who Ever Lived (2015)
